title: Two Sum and the hash map reflex
sub: Trade memory for time: from O(n²) to a single pass
cards/0/body:
Two Sum (LeetCode #1). Given an integer array nums and a number target, find two elements at different indices that add up to target and return their indices. On LeetCode there is exactly one answer, 2 ≤ n ≤ 10⁴, and the numbers and target are at most 10⁹ in absolute value.

In an interview this problem tests a reflex, not whether you remember Two Sum. Signals that a hash map will help:

1. For each element you look for a “partner” by exact value: the complement of a sum, the same number, the same anagram.
2. The question sounds like “have I seen this before?” or “how many times?”.
3. The array is unsorted, and sorting is expensive or not allowed: you need the original indices.

All three are here: the partner of x is exactly target − x, the question is “have I seen it?”, and the answer is indices.
cards/1/q: Which problems call for the same “have I seen this?” → hash map reflex? Select all.
cards/1/options/0: Does the array contain a number that appears at least twice
cards/1/options/1: Does the array contain two numbers whose difference is k
cards/1/options/2: The first non-repeating character of a string
cards/1/options/3: The largest sum of consecutive elements
cards/1/options/4: The k-th largest number in the array
cards/1/explain: A duplicate is “have I seen it before?” (signal 2). Difference k is a partner by exact value: for x look up x − k and x + k (signal 1). The first non-repeating character is “how many times?”: counters, then a second pass. The largest consecutive sum and the k-th largest are not about finding a partner by value: other techniques work there (a greedy pass, a heap, quickselect), covered in later units.
cards/2/title: The naive solution and its cost
cards/2/body:
The brute-force solution checks every pair i < j. There are n(n − 1)/2 pairs, so the time is O(n²) and the extra memory is O(1).

Put numbers on it. For n = 10⁵ there are 10⁵ · (10⁵ − 1) / 2 ≈ 5·10⁹ pairs. By the rule from the first unit, ~10⁸ simple operations per second, that is about 50 seconds against a 1–2 second limit: 25–50 times too slow.

A square grows fast: 10 times more data means 100 times more work. In an interview, always name the naive solution and its cost — it is your baseline.
cards/3/q: On LeetCode, Two Sum has n ≤ 10⁴. How many comparisons does the naive solution make in the worst case, and what follows from that?
cards/3/options/0: ≈ 5·10⁷ — fits the time limit, but the interviewer will ask for something faster than O(n²)
cards/3/options/1: ≈ 5·10⁹ — too slow, a different solution is required
cards/3/explain: n(n − 1)/2 for n = 10⁴ is about 5·10⁷: by the same rule (~10⁸ operations per second) that is a fraction of a second. That is why brute force passes on LeetCode, and the problem statement asks: can you do better than O(n²)? That step is exactly what the interview is waiting for.
cards/3/wrong/1: 5·10⁹ is for n = 10⁵. With 10 times smaller n the work is 100 times smaller: it is a square.
cards/3/wrong/2: 10⁴ is the number of elements, but we compare pairs. There are about n²/2 of them.
cards/4/body:
Look at the inner loop: for each nums[i] it searches for one specific value, target − nums[i] — and it starts over every time, scanning. Finding a value in an unsorted array is O(n). In a hash map it is O(1) on average.

Turn the problem around: walk left to right and for the current x ask “have I met target − x?”. Keep everything seen so far in a Dictionary<int, int>. The dictionary stores not “what was there” but “where it was”: the key is the number, the value is its index.

Invariant: before step i the dictionary holds exactly the elements nums[0..i−1]. So check first, then insert — otherwise x finds itself. Time O(n), memory O(n): we trade memory for time.

In a game: the same trade-off applies when an object is looked up by id with List.Find every frame — a Dictionary<int, Enemy> keyed by id answers in O(1).
cards/5/explain: We look for the complement need = target − nums[i]. TryGetValue answers “is it there?” and hands over the index j in a single lookup — j comes before i, so the answer is { j, i }. Then we remember the current number: seen[nums[i]] = i. The indexer, not Add: Add throws ArgumentException on a repeated key, for example on [1, 1, 5] with target = 10.
cards/6/task: Step through the trace on [3, 8, 2, 11, 7, 5], target = 9. The rig stops twice and asks what the code does next: answer from the dictionary on screen, not from the whole array.
cards/6/goal/asks/0/q: x = 2, looking for 7. The array does contain a 7. What does the code do?
cards/6/goal/asks/0/explain: The code only sees the dictionary, and so far it holds 3 and 8. The 7 is further right and not visited yet, so we store 2 → 2. The 7 will find the pair itself when we reach it: by then its partner 2 is already in the dictionary.
cards/6/goal/asks/1/q: x = 7, looking for 2. What does the code do?
cards/6/goal/asks/1/explain: 2 is in the dictionary at index 2 — TryGetValue finds it and returns j = 2. We return { j, i } = { 2, 4 }: the partner index first, then the current one. No need to store 7 any more.
cards/7/q: On nums = [3, 2, 4], target = 6 this code returns [0, 0]. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/7/explain: The number goes into the dictionary before the check, which breaks the invariant “the map holds only what is left of i”. At i = 0: seen[3] = 0, we look up 6 − 3 = 3 — and find the element itself, answer [0, 0]. This is the classic target = 2x trap. The fix is the order: TryGetValue first, then seen[nums[i]] = i.
cards/8/q: The dictionary solution (check first, then insert). What is true? Select all.
cards/8/options/1: Negative numbers and zero need no changes at all
cards/8/options/2: On a repeat, seen[x] = i overwrites the index, and the answer can get lost because of it
cards/8/options/3: With |nums[i]|, |target| ≤ 10⁹ the difference target − nums[i] overflows int
cards/8/options/4: If there is no pair, the loop ends and you return what was agreed on: an empty array or an exception
cards/8/explain: Duplicates: at i = 1 we look up 3, and 3 → 0 is already there — answer [0, 1]. The dictionary does not care what the keys are: negatives and zero just work. Overwriting is safe: any index of that value makes a valid pair, and a pair of two equal numbers is caught before the overwrite. No overflow: |target − x| ≤ 2·10⁹, and int.MaxValue = 2 147 483 647. If the numbers in the statement are wider, compute in long. What to return without a pair is a question for the interviewer at the very start.
cards/9/title: Variations: what changes in the statement
cards/9/body:
The array is sorted, memory O(1) (Two Sum II, #167; indices there are 1-based). No dictionary needed — two pointers moving towards each other: if the sum is too small, move the left one; if too large, the right one. A move loses nothing: if nums[lo] + nums[hi] < target, then nums[lo] gives a too-small sum with any smaller right element as well. O(n) time, O(1) memory. Details are in the two pointers unit.

How many pairs sum to target. A dictionary “value → how many times seen”: at each x first add count[target − x] to the answer, then increment count[x]. Still O(n).

A stream: add(x) and find(value) (Two Sum III, #170). If add is frequent and find is rare, keep counters: add is O(1), find walks the distinct keys, O(n); for x == value − x you need a count ≥ 2. If it is the other way round, keep a set of all pairwise sums: add is O(n), find is O(1), but memory is O(n²). Which operation is more frequent — ask the interviewer.

No index needed, only the fact (Contains Duplicate, #217): a HashSet<int>, and Add returns false if the number was already there.
cards/10/task: Step through Contains Duplicate on [4, 7, 1, 9, 7, 3]: each value goes into a HashSet in turn. The rig will stop and ask what the code does.
cards/10/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: Add(7) returns false — a repeat, return true
cards/10/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: Add(7) returns true and overwrites the 7
cards/10/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: Move on: without indices a HashSet cannot notice the repeat
cards/10/goal/asks/0/q: i = 4, nums[4] = 7. The set already holds 4, 7, 1 and 9. What does the code do?
cards/10/goal/asks/0/explain: The 7 is already in the set, so Add leaves the set as it is and returns false — that is the answer. A separate Contains before Add is not needed: the check and the insert are one hash lookup. No indices are needed either — the problem only asks whether a repeat exists.
cards/11/q: You solve Two Sum out loud in an interview. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
cards/11/items/0: Clarify: is there always an answer, can one element be used twice, what to return, what are n and the values
cards/11/items/1: Name the brute force over pairs: O(n²), about 5·10⁹ comparisons for n = 10⁵
cards/11/items/2: Idea: the brute force keeps searching for target − x; a “value → index” dictionary answers in O(1)
cards/11/items/3: Write the code while stating the invariant: the map holds everything left of i
cards/11/items/4: Run a small example out loud, such as [3, 2, 4] with target = 6
cards/11/items/5: State the complexity: O(n) time and O(n) memory
cards/11/items/6: Edge cases: no pair, duplicates, target = 2x, negative numbers
cards/11/explain: First agree on the statement, then the baseline (brute force and its cost), then the idea and the code, a check on an example, and only then complexity and edge cases. The [3, 2, 4] example also checks the 3 + 3 trap.
cards/12/title: Why a dictionary is O(1), and when it is not
cards/12/body:
The O(1) of a Dictionary is on average. A key lands in a bucket by its hash, and if keys are spread evenly, a bucket holds one or two entries.

Growth. When it runs out of room, the dictionary allocates arrays roughly twice as large and re-places every entry — that insert costs O(n). It happens rarely, so overall it is amortized O(1) per insert. If n is known in advance, set the capacity and there will be no re-placing.

The worst case is every key in one bucket: lookup is O(n), and Two Sum degrades to O(n²). For struct keys implement IEquatable<T> and GetHashCode, otherwise comparisons are slow and hashes are worse.
cards/12/code:
// n is known in advance: capacity up front, no re-placing
var seen = new Dictionary<int, int>(nums.Length);
cards/12/deep:
Internals. Dictionary<TKey,TValue> in .NET is two arrays: buckets (the number of the first entry in a chain) and entries (structs: hash, next, key, value). Lookup: key hash → bucket hash % buckets.Length → walk the next chain comparing the hash and Equals. The size is a prime; when full, the new size is a prime at least twice as large, and every entry is rehashed. The constructor without a capacity allocates no arrays — they appear on the first insert.

Collisions. The hash of an int is the number itself, so keys that all land in one bucket for a known table size can be picked on purpose. String hashing in .NET Core and .NET 5+ is randomized per process — a defence against collision attacks (hash flooding). So string.GetHashCode() must not be saved to disk, sent over the network, or used for determinism. In .NET Framework it is deterministic by default — code that relied on that breaks after migrating. The documentation does not guarantee the enumeration order of a dictionary either.

Struct keys. Without IEquatable<T> the default comparer calls Equals(object) — boxing on every comparison, and the default ValueType.Equals and GetHashCode may use reflection and may not take every field into account. Implement IEquatable<T> and GetHashCode; HashCode.Combine exists since .NET Core 2.1 and .NET Standard 2.1 (in Unity since 2021.2), but it is randomized per process too. The tuple (int, int) already implements IEquatable.

Allocations. new Dictionary is an object plus two arrays on the heap, and every re-placing means new arrays while the old ones become garbage. In hot code keep the dictionary in a field and call Clear(): the capacity stays, no new allocations.

Unity. The garbage collector is Boehm: no generations and no compaction, a collection walks the whole managed heap. Incremental mode spreads it across frames but does not cancel it. A new dictionary in Update is garbage every frame, so reuse it. Managed collections are unavailable in Jobs and Burst: NativeHashMap<TKey,TValue> from the com.unity.collections package — key and value are unmanaged, the key implements IEquatable<TKey>, memory lives outside the managed heap (Allocator.Temp, TempJob, Persistent) and is released with Dispose(). For writing from a parallel job use NativeParallelHashMap and its AsParallelWriter().

cards/13/pairs/0/1: Two pointers moving towards each other
cards/13/pairs/1/0: How many pairs sum to target
cards/13/pairs/2/0: A stream: add often, find rarely
